analytic.title: Augmenting sensitivity analysis for eme ded applications by program level derivation of process parameters

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: From the perspective of scheduling the design and development of real-time applications is straightforward. Given the software architecture in terms of a process model and the respective process parameters a variety of methods are available to decide whether the real-time constraints of an application are satisfied or not. However, in practice of application design and development we are unable to follow this straightforward principle. Instead, in the course of a project a lot of pragmatism, experience-based variation and systematic testing finally lead to acceptable solutions. More or less in the last decade those refinement steps have gained scientific interest and emerged towards the so called sensitivity analysis for real-time systems.

On one hand we are convinced that sensitivity analysis, as it is applied today, contributes valuable insights into the variation potential of an application-specific software architecture. On the other hand it is obvious that due to the architecturebased approach sensitivity analysis operates at the same level of abstraction as schedulability analysis does. So, both methods neglect lower levels of abstraction which are needed to derive process parameters, first of all execution times and periods. As there already exists a vast stock of methods for the derivation of execution times this paper focusses on the systematic calculation of periods. The approach operates on the abstraction level of pro- gramming and follows the objective that programmed actions are responsible for quality criterions in its application environment. To achieve this objective all time-and value-dependent deviations of sensor/actor systems and the computations system have to be formalized to be taken into account.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: The theory of real-time scheduling is strongly process- oriented and presumes the knowledge of various process- dependent parameters. The most important ones are the de- mand for execution time by a given process and the temporal constraints on its starting and completio(n times. The former is typically derived from experimental measurements or -more sophisticated -from a worst case execution time analysis of the program code executed by this process. A magnitude of research efforts have been spent to estimate the demand for execution time and several tools to perform this calculation for a given hardware are available today (see survey articles [17] and [5]).

In contrast it seems to us that the question of finding the time bounds in terms of deadlines or periods has not attracted the same degree of attention. The reason may be that real- time conditions for processes are not unique by themselves and depend upon a heterogeneity of criterions, e.g.- . The nature of the application environment consisting of some technical system which has to be controlled. . The time-and value dependent deviations emerging from the sensor and actuator systems to measure and influence the technical system. * The restrictions imposed by the infrastructure with re- spect to the granularity of time measurement. * The availability of certain scheduling policies for the execution of processes, e.g. available from the API of the underlying operation system. * The specified real-time conditions which have to be respected for the technical system and which have to be established at the level of programming. Sensitivity analysis as it is applied today does not cover these topics. A typical application context so far has focussed on the permissible changes of the worst case execution times (WCET) of processes, looking for scaling factors for the change of computation times which still keep the feasibility property for the whole set of processes (see e.g. [19] and [14]). Newer approaches also take deadlines and periods into account. However, their approach starts at the abstraction level of the process model and asks how feasibility can be apportioned to the quantitative variation of certain process parameters. Particular questions are on a global minimum period reduction applying the EDF scheduling policy (see [4]) or on the minimum deadline of certain tasks under a general dynamic scheduling policy (see [2X). Depending topics such as the reduction of jitter which is particularly important for control applications are also discussed in this context (see e.g.

In contrast to the approaches above our investigation starts at the lower abstraction level of programming So first in section 2 our program level approach is motivated from the perspective of our experiences and the few similar approaches in this context. Section 3 introduces a canonically structured compu- tational model for real-time control applications. Section 4 is 1-4244-0840-7/07/$20.00 02007 IEEE. of central importance in that it derives an operative calculus for limiting deviation in value and time. This calculus is applied to a very simple example in section 5. However, the sensitivity analysis applied to this example shows that things really are not so simple from the perspective of program development. Finally in section 6 the status of the approach and the potential tool support is assessed.

div.head: II. TOWARDS A PROGRAM LEVEL ABSTRACTION
div.p: The article is strongly motivated by our experience with embedded system developmnent in two different automotive application contexts. First of all there are our laboratory model trucks to simulate driving maneuvers, e.g. docking maneuvers to ramps for charging or discharging purposes. Collision- free maneuvering is guaranteed by a strict rule: There is exactly one two-dimensional shape which covers the entire vehicle, e.g. truck and trailer, for a certain interval of time. This is denoted in terms of an invariant property which has to be guaranteed by the computational system, in this case programmed actions which control speed and steering angle (see [23]). The other scope of automotive application regards driver assistance, particularly driver assistance for backing up cars with trailers. Here a backward camera image is transmitted to a display mounted on the dashboard augmented with trajectories where car and trailer will take in the future given the current steering wheel (see figure 2). Also here an invariant property guarantees that the anticipated motion of the articulated ve- hicle will be covered by a certain two-dimensional tolerance shape, taking into account all time-and value-based deviations of the embedded solution (see [3]).

A basic attempt towards the formulation of real-time conditions has been adopted from the modelling techniques applied forr database systems. Instead of the value based definition of consistency, real-time applications require some temporal version of consistency, accentuating that real-time processes operate on data objects that are steadily aging (see [1] and [15])J The two decisive definitions -absolute and relative temporal consistency -bound the absolute and relative time since the data has been taken from the real world.

A generalization of this approach to determine real time conditions distinguishes between the technical system, re- presented in terms of real-time entities, and its observation, Fig. 2. Angle measurement for a driving assistant system to back up car and trailer.

namely real-time images [10]. A relation, called temporal accuracy, is defined for assigning the real-time image to some real-time entity within a bound history. Based on this knowledge the worst case error when utilizing this real-time iimage is estiiiated and caii be taken into accouuit for decisionis which have to be made by the real-time process.

Our article may be understood as an attempt to continue the approaches cited above. The reason to do so is at least threefold in that we try to overcome shortcomings and extend these approaches to achieve a surplus in the integration into the software development cycle. First, let us have a look at the shortcomings that we feel.
. The knowledge of some current time t is assumed. However, the execution of processes is prone to jitter.

This holds for the startilng (and completion) times of subsequent process executions, but even more subtle also for subsequent statements within the same execution of a process. So, the utmost knowledge we assume here is the duration of the time interval where the statements of the process are executed sequentially, but potentially interrupted at any instant of time. * Only the history up to some current time t is considered.

However, the process controlling the technical system has to make decisions which have consequences for the future. This has to be a.nticipated with some bound degree of deviation and fed back to the technical system. The methods to be used here are analogous to those used for the history. * The approaches concentrate on inaccuracies in time. However, the inaccuracy of the values must not be neglected.

Furthermore, it has to be considered that there can be a tradeoff between the inaccuracies of time and value. Besides these shortcomings and before proposing our approach we take a brief look at the development of time-critical software from the viewpoint of a programmer Typically this viewpoint is program-centric in that the values of variables are processed and evaluated for decision making. Particularly in the scope of embedded systems several questions emerge from this view and unsettle the programmer v How precise is the value of a variable in correlation to the technical system? . From which instant of time with respect to the technical system does the value of a variable stem? . At which instant of time a decision will be made by the program in execution? * At which instant of time will the decision made by the program take effect in the technical system. Program code written under these circumstances is aggregated to processes which build up the computational part of the embedded system. These processes are executed concurrently following some real-time scheduling policy. Even though there is a profound theory of scheduling behind, the question remains how to extract the application-specific time bounds in order to apply this theory.

As far as we see only a few articles adopt a similar point of view: seeing the programmer in a role to control a technical system by a computational system prone to deficiencies in time and value (e.g. see [6], [16] and [13]). The article which is nearest to ours is the approach of Verissimo and Casimiro [18].

Similarities are in that also some canonical process model, the sentient object metaphor, is the fundamental abstraction for processing. This metaphor is seamlessly applied to both the technical and the computational system constituting the embedded system. Also similar is the abstraction which is used to distinguish between the entity of the technical system and its computational image prone to deficiency in time and value. However, their approach does not go further than postulating a bounded error that has be established somehow.

Independently of the deliberations of Verlssimo and Casimiro our approach aims at the effective computation of application specific time bounds for canonical processes. To achieve this in a comprehensive but straightforward way we favor in contrast to the authors above strictly time-triggered canonical processes. Based on this a method is developed which takes the specification in terms of the technical system, considers pessimistic deficiencies in time and value of the computational image and computes the time bounds for the canonical processes, as far as they exist.

In a next step our approach not only refers to a single canonical process. Typically the computational part of an em- bedded system requires complex processing involving several processes. For the sake of acceptance by programmers the time bounds of single canonical processes should be combinable in a simple fashion. Due to this aspect a technique of propagating time bounds is applied which is based on age constraint processes (see [2I], [1I] and [22]). This approach does not achieve the utmost degree of utilization, but combines a lot of favorable properties with respect to the clarity of software design and the derivation of feasibility criterions.

To sum up our approach starts from a program level abstrac- tion. Systematically all time-and value-dependent deviations that may exist at the execution time of the program code are taken into account Furthermore a correlation to the goal of the real-time is established. This correlation considers on one hand the objective of the real time aoplication and on the other hand what really may happen in the program, Therefore the objective is expressed in terms of an invariant property of the technical system. In a step by step fashion this invariant is transformed to a corresponding, canonically structured program-code guaranteeing the compliance of the invariant.

div.head: III. THE CANONICAL STRUCTURE OF THE COMPUTATIONAL SYSTEM
div.p: The majority of real-time applications center around the control of at least one technical system. The control itself is established by a computational system which gathers infor- mation about the technical system, condenses this information in order to assess the status which the technical system is in. Then, depending upon this assessment control decisions have to be taken and corresponding actions have to be initiated. The decision and initiation is henceforth called control action CA.

The control action is piece of program code. So, the question arises on what a developer can trust when referring to the variables which are to represent the status of the technical system at the instant of execution. For an accurate consideration we introduce a basic model of control (see figure 3) which distinguishes between the set of value domains V = {V1, ..., V,} describing the technical system and the set OV = {OV OV,°} of domains constituting the observed images of these values. VI. CONCLUSION AND OUTLOOK This work wants to be understood as a consequent and sophisticated enhancement of those papers which already have modelled value-and time-dependent imprecisions of real-time systems (e.g. [1], [10] or [18]). Even at the lowest level of abstraction -the coding of statements which interfere with the technical system to be controlled -the topics of scheduling and verification can be combined. On one hand the formulas derived in this paper are elaborate or even bulky to be handled literally. On the other hand they have a clear structure and they are applicable forward and backward. Furthermore additional knowledge can be used in a pragmatic fashion for the simplification of the calculations. We know that the example chosen to demonstrate the cal- culus is too simple to represent typical real-time applications. Nevertheless it shows the inherent complexity which emerges from the programmer's perspective, taking into account all sensor-, program-and actuator-dependant value-and time- deviations. Furthermore, the static formulation for the behavior of the technical system is extremely restrictive. Instead of invariants some type of dynamic formulation is needed to describe the controllability properties of control applications. Relating program-code of the computational system to the physical entities of the technical system and thereby deriving deadlines has been the main focus of our approach. In this it is a first approach (as far as we know) to relate the programming level with both schedulability analysis and sensitivity analysis (see figure 7 which depicts the data flow perspective of our approach). In contrast to the majority of the other approaches we know, our approach can be characterized as one which primarily focusses on the later steps of software development, because we believe that here is an even higher demand for support than in the early phases. Typically the real-time software is prone to a myriad of changes when implemented, integrated, tested or even when it is running in its environments. So, there is a great need to keep some kind of synchrony (a metaphor used by [12]) between the computational and the technical system. Keeping this synchrony manually -as we do today -is not acceptable and shows the prototypic status of our approach. Consequently, we look for possibilities to integrate our formalism into those tools which principally allow to insert assertions in programs (there are some) and -up to now -do not have the right formalisms to generate them.
